title: "31 - Data Visualization: Male vs. Female SUD and MDE"

  html_document:
    df_print: paged

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
source("00_requirements.R")   # loads packages
source("02_funct_Plots.R")    # loads plotting functions
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)   # folder where figures are saved
```

## 1. Load the data

The data come from Appendix Table 1 of the SAMHSA NSDUH Short Report
(March 2026), annual averages for 2022-2024. Counts are in thousands.

```{r load-data}
sex_data <- read_csv("data/nsduh_table1_sex.csv")

sex_data <- sex_data %>%
  mutate(sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
         age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("Adolescents (12-17)", "Adults (18+)")),
         outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("SUD", "MDE", "Co-occurring SUD and MDE")))

glimpse(sex_data)
```

## 2. Numerical summary

```{r summary-table}
diff_data <- compute_sex_differences(sex_data)

diff_data %>%
  transmute(`Age group` = age_group, Outcome = outcome,
            `Male (%)` = percentage_Male, `Female (%)` = percentage_Female,
            `Diff F-M (pp)` = round(diff_pp, 1),
            `Ratio F/M` = round(ratio_F_to_M, 2)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Past-year prevalence by sex, NSDUH 2022-2024")
```

## 3. Prevalence by sex

Grouped bars compare male and female prevalence for each outcome, with 95%
confidence intervals. Non-overlapping intervals indicate a clear difference.

```{r plot-prevalence, fig.height=4.5}
fig1 <- plot_sex_comparison(sex_data, "Past-year SUD and MDE by sex")
ggsave("figures/fig1_prevalence_by_sex.png", fig1, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
fig1
```

**Interpretation:** Among adults, males have a higher SUD prevalence than
females (21.4% vs. 14.6%), which supports our hypothesis. Among adolescents,
the pattern reverses: females are higher for SUD (9.9% vs. 6.8%), and far
higher for MDE (26.0% vs. 9.8%). The confidence intervals do not overlap in
any comparison, so all differences are clear.

## 4. Number of people affected

```{r plot-counts, fig.height=4.5}
fig2 <- plot_counts(sex_data, "Estimated number of people with SUD/MDE by sex")
ggsave("figures/fig2_counts_by_sex.png", fig2, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
fig2
```

**Interpretation:** Adult males account for about 26.9 million people with an
SUD versus 19.4 million adult females, so the larger percentage also means
a larger absolute burden.

## 5. Size of the gender gap

```{r plot-difference}
fig3 <- plot_sex_difference(diff_data, "Female - male difference in prevalence")
ggsave("figures/fig3_sex_difference.png", fig3, width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300)
fig3
```

**Interpretation:** Points left of zero mean higher prevalence in males;
points right of zero mean higher in females. Adult SUD is the only outcome
where males are clearly higher. Every other outcome is higher for females.

## 6. Planned further visualizations

- Female-only breakdowns (poverty level, education, employment) from
  Tables 2-4 of the report.
- Suicidality and SUD severity by SUD/MDE status (Tables 5-7).
- Opioid-specific data from the full NSDUH public-use files, since this
  short report covers SUD in general.
